title: AWS EDP: What Marketplace Sellers Need to Know
summary: AWS EDP explained for sellers: how the Enterprise Discount Program works, how AWS Marketplace purchases draw down committed spend, and why it wins deals.
body_text: An AWS EDP is a committed-spend agreement in which a customer promises AWS a level of spend over a term in exchange for discounts — and because eligible AWS Marketplace purchases draw it down, it quietly shapes how your enterprise buyers prefer to buy. When an enterprise prospect asks “can we put this on our AWS bill?”, there’s usually an EDP behind the question. Most sellers hear a procurement preference. What’s actually driving it is a budget the customer has already committed to spend. The EDP is a buyer-side agreement — you aren’t a party to it — but it changes the economics of every deal you run with that customer. Purchases that draw down the commitment are, in effect, money the buyer has to spend anyway. Here’s what an EDP is, how marketplace purchases interact with it, and what it means for the way you sell. What is an AWS EDP? An AWS EDP (Enterprise Discount Program) is a private, negotiated agreement between AWS and a customer in which the customer commits to spend a minimum amount on AWS over a multi-year term, and AWS provides discounts in return. It’s a buyer-side contract — the discount rewards the customer’s committed spend, and it scales with the size of the commitment. From the buyer’s side, the point of an EDP is predictable pricing at scale. A company running large workloads on AWS trades some flexibility for a better rate: they promise a spend floor, and AWS discounts against it. As a software seller, you are not a party to the EDP. But you sell to companies that have one, and that changes what they want from you. How do AWS Marketplace purchases draw down an EDP? Eligible AWS Marketplace purchases count toward a customer’s EDP commitment. When a customer buys your software through AWS Marketplace, that spend generally applies to the amount they’ve already committed to spend with AWS. That’s the mechanic that matters. A third-party software purchase made through the marketplace isn’t separate from the customer’s AWS relationship — it flows through it. So the dollars a buyer spends on your product can do double duty: they buy your software and they retire part of a commitment the buyer has to meet regardless. Buying the same software outside the marketplace — a direct contract, a separate invoice — does none of that. The spend sits outside the EDP, and the commitment still has to be met some other way. Why does an EDP make marketplace the preferred buying path? For a customer with an EDP, buying through the marketplace turns a cost into progress toward an obligation they’ve already signed up for. Every eligible dollar spent in the marketplace is a dollar they don’t have to find elsewhere to hit their commitment — which is why procurement teams at EDP accounts often steer purchases onto the marketplace by default. This is the part sellers underestimate. When an enterprise buyer asks to transact on AWS Marketplace, it’s frequently not a preference — it’s direction from finance to route spend through the committed channel. A vendor who can’t sell that way creates friction against the buyer’s own budget structure. The implication: marketplace eligibility isn’t a billing detail. For EDP accounts, it can be the difference between an easy yes and a procurement escalation. What does an EDP mean for you as a seller? It means you should make your software easy to buy the way EDP customers want to buy — through the marketplace, on terms that fit an enterprise deal. Two moves do most of the work. First, be marketplace-eligible: list and sell on AWS Marketplace so an EDP customer can transact with you through the channel that draws down their commitment. If you’re new to the mechanics, start with AWS Marketplace for sellers . Second, use private offers for anything beyond a standard public price. Enterprise deals rarely close at list — they close at a negotiated price, a custom term and a payment schedule. Private offers on the marketplace let you deliver that negotiated deal through the marketplace, so it still counts toward the buyer’s EDP while matching the commercial terms you agreed. Put together: the buyer gets EDP drawdown and a negotiated price, and you get a closed deal instead of a procurement standoff. How does an EDP compare to Azure and Google Cloud? Every major cloud has a committed-spend program, and each counts eligible marketplace purchases toward the commitment. The names differ; the mechanic is the same. Cloud Committed-spend program Marketplace draws it down? AWS Enterprise Discount Program (EDP) Yes Microsoft Azure Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC) Yes Google Cloud Committed-spend / consumption agreements Yes The takeaway holds across all three hyperscalers: enterprise buyers with a commitment prefer to buy software through the marketplace that draws it down. For the Microsoft side, we cover the Azure equivalent, a MACC in depth. What do sellers get wrong about EDPs? The most common mistake is treating an EDP as purely the buyer’s problem. It shapes your deal whether or not you engage with it, so ignoring it just means being surprised by it. A few others are worth clearing up: “An EDP discounts my software.” No. The discount applies to the customer’s AWS spend, not your price. Your pricing stays yours to set. “The customer needs a massive AWS footprint.” EDPs do skew toward larger accounts with meaningful multi-year commitments, but the drawdown mechanic — marketplace spend counting toward the commitment — matters to any buyer who already has one, not only the very largest. “Marketplace takes a cut, so it’s worse for me.” The listing fee is usually outweighed by faster enterprise deals and access to committed budget — especially on private offers. Frequently asked questions What is an AWS EDP? An AWS Enterprise Discount Program (EDP) is a negotiated agreement where a customer commits to a minimum level of AWS spend over a multi-year term in exchange for discounts. It’s a buyer-side contract between AWS and the customer. Do AWS Marketplace purchases count toward an EDP? Yes. Eligible AWS Marketplace purchases generally draw down a customer’s EDP commitment, which is why enterprise buyers with an EDP often prefer to buy third-party software through the marketplace rather than on a direct contract. Does an EDP give me a discount as a seller? No. An EDP discounts the customer’s AWS spend, not your software price. You set your own pricing. Private offers let you deliver a negotiated price through the marketplace while the purchase still draws down the buyer’s commitment. Should I list on AWS Marketplace because of EDPs? If you sell to enterprises, yes. Marketplace eligibility lets EDP customers apply their purchase to committed spend they have to meet anyway — often turning a procurement debate into a straightforward approval. Do Azure and Google Cloud have an EDP equivalent? Yes. Azure has the Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC) and Google Cloud has committed-spend agreements. Both count eligible marketplace purchases toward the commitment, the same way an AWS EDP does. Takeaways An EDP is a buyer-side commitment between AWS and a customer — you’re not a party to it, but it shapes every deal you run with that customer. Eligible AWS Marketplace purchases draw down the commitment, which is why EDP customers prefer to buy software through the marketplace. Be marketplace-eligible and use private offers, so an enterprise buyer gets EDP drawdown and a negotiated price in one transaction. The pattern repeats on Azure and Google Cloud — committed spend plus marketplace drawdown is now the default enterprise buying path. title: Zero-rated vs Exempt Supplies in the UAE
summary: Exempt and zero-rated supplies in the UAE are not subject to VAT but differ in input tax claim rights. Read on to learn more about their essential features.
body_text: Have you ever felt like the world of taxes speaks a whole different language? You're not alone. Things can get a bit confusing, especially when it comes to VAT (Value Added Tax). But don’t worry – we have a handy guide to help you with your VAT process. In this article, we will discuss the concepts of exempt and zero-rated supplies in the UAE. We will also examine their impact on VAT reporting, the significance of Form VAT201, and how understanding VAT can contribute to your business’s financial strategy. ‍ What is the VAT rule in the UAE? In the UAE, VAT is applicable at a standard rating of 5% tax . It is an indirect tax applicable on the supply of most goods and services, including imports. As a VAT-registered business, you must collect the tax on outward supplies (sales). You need to transfer this amount to the Federal Tax Authority (FTA) after deducting the VAT paid on your inward supplies (purchases). Here is an example to help you better understand the VAT rules in the UAE . Suppose you are running a furniture business and buy wood for AED 1000. The VAT on this purchase is AED 50 (5% of AED 1,000). You manufacture a table and sell it for AED 2,000. The VAT on this sale is AED 100 (5% of AED 2,000). As a VAT-registered business, you collect AED 100 from your customer, but you have already paid AED 50 as VAT on your raw materials. So, you deduct this AED 50 from the AED 100 collected; the remaining AED 50 is what you remit to the FTA. Understanding UAE VAT Law can help you maintain FTA compliance and ensure accurate financial reporting to avoid possible penalties or fines. UAE VAT Law also specifies exempt and zero-rated supplies that must be handled differently than the standard VAT—more details on this will be provided in our following sections. ‍ What are zero-rated supplies in the UAE As per the UAE VAT rules , zero-rated supplies in the UAE are goods or services that are subject to VAT but at a rate of 0%. Simply put, You don't collect any VAT from your customers on these supplies. You can claim the input tax credit for any VAT you paid on expenses related to those supplies. Think of it like this: you are providing a service, but the government says, "hey, this one's important, keep the tax money you paid for supplies." This can be a significant cost-saver for businesses that deal in zero-rated supplies. ‍ Here are the zero-rated supplies mentioned in the UAE VAT Law: Export of services and goods outside the GCC : Export of goods and services outside the GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) are taxed at 0%. International transportation services : International transport services for passengers or goods are subject to a zero VAT rate. This includes related supplies like pallets, crates, safety equipment, etc. Specific means of transport : The sale or lease of trains, trams, vessels, and aeroplanes qualify as zero-rated supplies in the UAE. Precious metals : Import of precious metals like silver, gold, and platinum is taxable at 0%. The metal purity must be 99 per cent or more, and it should be in a form that is tradable in global bullion markets. Residential buildings : The first sale or rent of residential buildings intended and designed for human use is zero-rated. Charity-related buildings : Buildings specifically designed to be used by charities also qualify as zero-rated supplies in the UAE. Certain educational services : Some educational services and related goods and services are zero-rated under the UAE VAT rules. These include, Nursery, preschool, and school education. Higher education by institutions that are either owned by the government or funded by more than 50% of the government. The educational institution must be recognised by the competent federal or local government and follow the government-approved curriculum. Only the core educational services and directly related goods and services qualify for zero-rated VAT. Any educational services offered by entities other than those mentioned above will be charged at a 5% standard rate. Specific healthcare services : The following healthcare services and related goods and services qualify for zero VAT. Curative and preventive healthcare services, including treatments, diagnoses, consultations, and procedures performed by licensed medical professionals. Services provided by hospitals and clinics (government and private). This also includes licensed medical practitioners (doctors, nurses, dentists, etc.) authorised by the Ministry Of Health And Prevention (MOHAP) or other relevant authorities. Certain medical equipment and medication can also be zero-rated when included in a list approved by the UAE Cabinet and supplied specifically for use in combination with zero-rated healthcare services. Criteria for zero-rated VAT treatment: The healthcare service must be generally accepted in the medical field as necessary for the patient's treatment, including preventive measures. The good or service must be directly linked to the zero-rated healthcare service . For example, if a specific medication is crucial for a treatment covered under zero-rated VAT, the medication itself might also be zero-rated. Services like cosmetic treatments or those not directly related to medical care typically don't qualify for zero-rated VAT and are subject to a 5% standard VAT rate. What are exempt supplies? Exempt supplies are certain goods and services on which VAT is not charged at the time of the supply. Unlike zero-rated supplies, if you supply exempt goods or services, you cannot recover any tax incurred on the related expenses. Knowing what qualifies as exempt supplies might help you manage your VAT accounting effectively. ‍ Here are the exempt supplies specified under the UAE VAT law: Bare land : The supply of bare land enjoys VAT exemption in the UAE. If you deal with the sale of vacant land, you cannot levy any tax on these transactions. Financial services : Some financial services that do not involve direct payment are exempt from VAT. The payment could be in the form of fees, commissions, discounts, rebates, or similar compensations. This exemption also applies to services such as life insurance and life reinsurance. Local transport services : If you supply local passenger transport services within the UAE, then these transactions are exempt from VAT. This rule applies to businesses operating taxis, buses, trains, or ferries. Lease or rent of residential properties : Residential buildings other than those specifically zero-rated are exempt from VAT. This means if you are in the business of selling or renting residential properties, you need not charge any tax. Non-recoverable input tax The term ‘non-recoverable input tax’ refers to the VAT that your company incurs on certain purchases and expenses but may not claim any input credit for it. You cannot deduct this VAT amount when calculating your net VAT payable. Here are the different expense categories where it is not possible to claim input VAT credit: Entertainment services Provided to non-employees : If you treat clients, potential customers, or shareholders to entertainment, the VAT incurred here is not recoverable. This applies to meals, events, or any activity considered entertainment as per the VAT rules. Business vehicle usage : If your business owns or leases vehicles that are available for private use by anyone (including employees), the VAT on these expenses is generally not recoverable. However, if the vehicle is used exclusively for business purposes, you can recover the VAT, subject to certain conditions. Goods or services purchased for employees : If you purchase any goods or services for employees’ personal use (beyond what is required for employment), the VAT incurred on these expenses is not recoverable. Such expenses include perks like staff outings, gifts, and club memberships. Entertainment services and personal vehicle use are covered here in brief — see the dedicated breakdown of what else falls into this category . Understanding VAT declaration (Form VAT201) The VAT Declaration (Form VAT201) is a crucial part of your VAT compliance in the UAE. It is a document you submit to the FTA detailing your VAT activity for a specific period . Filing this form accurately and timely can help you avoid any possible penalties and ensure smooth tax operations. You can follow these steps to access Form VAT201: Visit the FTA’s e-Services portal and log in to your account. If you do not have an account, complete the registration for a new account first. Once logged in, you can find the form under the ‘VAT’ tab. Select ‘VAT201 - VAT Return’ to start the process. Filling out Form VAT201 requires careful attention. Depending on the nature of business activities, you may be required to provide the following details: Your Tax Registration Number (TRN) The reporting period (usually quarterly) Details of your taxable supplies and their value (excluding VAT) Details of zero-rated supplies and exempt supplies (if applicable) Details of your expenses and the amount of input tax you can claim By accurately reporting these figures, you can ensure that you pay only the net amount of VAT due. Try to maintain organised financial records throughout the reporting period to streamline the filing process for Form VAT201. Expense management software like Alaan can automate the process of maintaining and organising your financial records , making it easier to report figures for Form VAT201 accurately. Alaan also helps you track and categorise expenses, ensuring that the input tax claim is accurate and that only the net amount of VAT due is paid. For the full VAT201 filing walkthrough beyond just this declaration form, see the complete filing guide . Do businesses have to register under VAT UAE if they fall under zero-rated supplies? Even if your company mainly deals in zero-rated supplies in the UAE, you may still need to register for VAT, as the registration criterion is based on the taxable turnover of the business. If the taxable turnover of your enterprise exceeds AED 375,000 in a 12-month period, it is advisable to register for VAT within 30 days of crossing the specified threshold. In this context, taxable turnover refers to both standard (5%) and zero-rated supplies (0%). Therefore, it is recommended that you keep track of your taxable turnover regularly and register for VAT as necessary. Exception for Solely Zero-Rated Supplies There is a potential exception to the above rule. Suppose your business deals only in zero-rated supplies (such as airlines, hospitals, exports, etc.) and makes no standard VAT-rated supplies. In that case, you can apply for a VAT registration exemption. However, it shall be subject to the following conditions: This exemption needs to be approved by the FTA. With this exemption, you need not submit regular VAT returns. You shall not be able to recover any input tax paid on business purchases. Impact of exempt and zero-rated supplies on businesses Understanding how exempt and zero-rated supplies impact your business can play an important role in VAT compliance and financial planning. Here is an analysis of the key aspects: VAT registration The choice to register for VAT is influenced by the type of supplies you provide. Exempt Supplies : As per the rules, if your enterprise deals only in exempt supplies, then you need not register for VAT. Zero-Rated Supplie s: On the other hand, if your enterprise exceeds the AED 375,000 taxable turnover threshold (including zero-rated supplies), you must register for VAT. You can consider registering for VAT if your turnover crosses the voluntary registration threshold of AED 187,500 during the tax period. While you do not charge any VAT on the sales, you can claim input tax credit on qualifying business expenses. This could lead to significant cost savings and boost your profits. Filing returns Even with exempt or zero-rated supplies, VAT filing requirements still apply. Here is the key difference: Exempt Supplies: You need to report the value of your exempt supplies in the VAT return. However, you cannot claim any input tax related to those supplies. Zero-Rated Supplies: You must report the value of zero-rated supplies in your VAT return. You are eligible to claim input tax credit on qualifying expenses related to those zero-rated supplies. Financial management The impact on your finances depends on the type of supplies: Exempt Supplies: As you cannot claim input tax on exempt supplies, your overall costs might be higher compared to zero-rated supplies. The VAT you pay on business expenses is an added cost that cannot be recovered through VAT returns. Zero-Rated Supplies: The ability to claim input tax on zero-rated supplies can be a significant financial benefit. You may recover the VAT paid on expenses incurred while providing those supplies. This can lead to cost reduction and potentially better profit margins. Conclusion Well, this is all we have for today. To summarise quickly, VAT is applied to most goods and services sold within the UAE. But there are some exceptions – exempt supplies and zero-rated supplies . Understanding the difference between these two can save you a VAT headache (and maybe even some money!). As a business, it is beneficial to have a tool that simplifies finance and helps you calculate accurate taxes. This is where an expense management platform helps! title: FedEx Helps Thai Businesses Adapt Confidently to EU De Minimis Changes
summary: Expands digital tools, expert guidance, and connectivity to help Thai businesses manage compliance and sustain growth
body_text: BANGKOK, THAILAND, July 2, 2026 — Federal Express Corporation (FedEx), one of the world’s largest express transportation companies, is strengthening its support for APAC businesses as they prepare for the European Union’s removal of the de minimis duty exemption on July 1, 2026. The policy change is expected to introduce stricter customs requirements and higher compliance costs for cross-border shipments into Europe. Ahead of the implementation, FedEx engaged more than 5,000 businesses across 12 Asia Pacific markets, through a series of customer education webinars hosted by FedEx, supporting organizations from small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to multinationals with practical guidance to navigate evolving customs clearance requirements, maintain operational efficiency, and reduce the risk of unexpected costs in an increasingly complex trade environment. “Europe remains a key market for Thai businesses, accounting for 7.2% of total bilateral trade, worth €44.3 billion (THB 1.6 trillion) in 2025. The upcoming removal of the EU de minimis duty exemption underscores the importance of compliance readiness in maintaining business competitiveness,” said Sasathorn Phaspinyo, managing director, FedEx Thailand. “FedEx remains committed to supporting Thai businesses through our trade expertise, digital tools, and reliable logistics solutions to help them adapt quickly, manage documentation requirements, reduce the risk of delays and unexpected costs, and continue capturing opportunities across Europe with greater confidence.” Awareness high, readiness uneven Survey results reveal strong awareness of the EU de minimis changes, but a notable gap between awareness and readiness remains: · Just over half, or 59% of APAC businesses, report being fully or mostly prepared, while 41% remain at an early stage or unprepared · Key barriers include: o Limited access to clear, actionable guidance (27%) o Lack of internal expertise on EU customs regulations (24%) o Difficulty keeping pace with evolving rules and timelines (22%) Businesses that are not fully prepared for new product data requirements, product identifiers, EU-wide handling fees, and stricter documentation standards may face delays at EU borders once the changes take effect. Businesses recalibrate cost and trade Rising compliance requirements and cost pressures are prompting businesses to reassess their approach to European markets. Forty-five percent of respondents cite EU customs regulations as a constraint to growth, driven by higher landed costs (24%) and increased compliance burdens (23%). More than one-third (36%) have already adjusted or plan to adjust their EU pricing, while half say the changes are influencing their trade corridor strategies, leading to a reassessment of market priorities. Among those diversifying beyond Europe, Intra-Asia (28%) and the United States (23%) are emerging as key alternatives, highlighting the importance of strong regional and global logistics connectivity. Support to navigate regulatory change FedEx is expanding support to help Thai customers stay compliant and keep shipments moving: 1. Digital systems aligned to new requirements · With 29% of businesses identifying digital customs and compliance tools as a top priority, FedEx shipping, invoicing, and clearance platforms are already aligned to meet new EU customs processes and data requirements, helping customers continue to ship with confidence. 2. Practical guidance and expert access As 25% of businesses seek clearer, step-by-step regulatory guidance, FedEx has launched a proactive customer support program including: · Direct outreach and detailed guides on Product Identifier (PID) requirements and the Import One-Stop Shop (IOSS). · Access to FedEx clearance and compliance specialists for support on classification, documentation and customs processes. · A dedicated EU de minimis information page across APAC markets with regularly updated guidance, videos, and trade resources. 3. Strengthening Asia-Europe connectivity To support continued trade across the critical Asia–Europe corridor, FedEx is enhancing network capacity and flexibility, including: · Five additional weekly flights between Asia and Europe, have been added in the past year, providing greater capacity and routing flexibility. · A total of 26 weekly flights supporting APAC to Europe shipments, enabling express deliveries in as little as 48 hours. Enabling continuity in a changing trade environment As businesses adapt to new regulatory realities, FedEx remains focused on ensuring continuity, helping customers stay compliant, manage costs, and maintain reliable access to European markets. To access the latest EU compliance guidance and support resources, businesses are encouraged to visit the FedEx Go-To Europe Hub and contact their local FedEx representative for personalized support. About the findings The insights in this release are based on feedback gathered from participants of FedEx customer webinars conducted in April & May 2026 across 12 Asia Pacific markets: Singapore, Philippines, Malaysia, Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Thailand, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and China. The webinars collectively engaged more than 5,000 customers, with over 500 survey responses gathered from participants representing businesses of varying sizes and industries.

title: Threat Hunting as a Service for MSPs and IT Teams
summary: Learn how threat hunting as a service works, its key benefits, and how to choose the right provider for your MSP or IT team.
body_text: A Ryuk-style intrusion can sit quietly inside a client environment for weeks, authenticating with stolen credentials, moving laterally, and staging data for exfiltration. No alerts fire because the attacker is using valid logins and native system tools. Finding that adversary before detonation requires active hunting. Threat hunting as a service (THaaS) is a managed security service where external analysts proactively search for adversaries who have already bypassed automated defenses, using hypothesis-driven investigation across endpoints, networks, and identity systems. The play here is closing the gap between attacker access and discovery without building a 24/7 SOC internally . N‑able has spent years supporting MSPs and IT teams and analyzing security events at scale, and THaaS puts dedicated analysts and specialized tooling behind that active search. The sections below walk through what THaaS delivers, how it works, the financial case, and how to evaluate providers. Why Your Team Needs Threat Hunting Signature-based detection and alert-driven monitoring catch known threats. Threat hunting finds the adversaries those tools miss, and the gap is widening. Attackers are getting stealthier. Living-off-the-land techniques are now used by 76% of nation-state actors, 59% of ransomware groups, and 44% of espionage attackers ( SANS survey ). Valid logins look legitimate to automated detection. Security information and event management ( SIEM ) rules and endpoint detection and response ( EDR ) policies cannot flag what they have no rule to recognize. When adversaries blend into normal administrative traffic using native tools like PowerShell, certutil, and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), hypothesis-driven hunting mapped to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK becomes the established practice for finding what standard detections miss. Here’s why that matters: global median dwell time has risen to 14 days in the most recent reporting period, driven by stealthy, long-term access campaigns ( Mandiant report ). Controls alone leave visibility gaps, especially when attacker behavior resembles normal administration. How Threat Hunting as a Service Works Threat hunting follows a structured lifecycle, whether the function is handled internally or by a managed security services provider. The engagement starts with environment profiling: the provider maps assets, data flows, user behavior baselines, and applicable threat actors for each client environment. Scheduled deep hunts run weekly, monthly, or quarterly, driven by new threat intelligence and advisories. Between scheduled hunts, continuous automated monitoring handles data collection, baseline comparison, and anomaly flagging for analyst review. What this looks like in practice: a hypothesis might target a healthcare client where recent sector-specific intelligence suggests PowerShell-based lateral movement consistent with known APT tactics. Analysts query PowerShell execution logs, WMI activity, and process lineage data across that client’s endpoints. Confirmed or partially confirmed findings generate new detection rules that automate future identification of that same behavior. This converts a one-time hunt into a repeatable detection. The play here is the feedback loop between hunting and detection. Every hunt investment compounds over time because findings become automated detections. Automation handles data collection, indicator of compromise (IoC) sweeps across all tenants simultaneously, and anomaly scoring. Human analysts handle hypothesis generation, novel technique identification, and the judgment call on whether anomalies are malicious or benign. Key Components and Benefits of Threat Hunting as a Service THaaS combines analyst-led hunting, automated monitoring, and reusable detections to improve coverage without adding internal headcount. A complete offering pairs threat intelligence feeds with skilled human analysts who execute MITRE ATT&CK playbooks and deliver compliance-ready reporting. The upshot: the financial case favors outsourced hunting. Faster detection can reduce breach impact, and THaaS delivers that advantage without the staffing burden. For MSPs, the operational benefit goes further. Cross-client visibility means the provider can translate findings from one environment into hunt coverage across others faster than a single-client deployment likely could. Threat Hunting as a Service vs. In-House Hunting The staffing math rarely works for in-house hunting. Building an internal hunting capability means paying for salaries and benefits before adding SIEM, EDR, threat intelligence feeds, and network detection tooling. THaaS providers amortize those platform and staffing costs across their entire client base, a structural advantage single organizations cannot match. Dimension In-House THaaS Annual staffing cost Multiple security hires required to sustain hunting coverage No dedicated internal full-time hire for hunting Tooling cost Additional SIEM, EDR, and threat intelligence spend Often included in service 24/7 coverage Requires shift scheduling most small teams cannot sustain Typically included by provider Time to become operational Typically months to hire, onboard, and build workflows Typically weeks Cross-client intelligence Limited to one organization’s telemetry Across the provider’s client base For MSPs, a co-managed model offers a fast path. The THaaS provider handles detection and hunting while the MSP manages client relationships and escalation coordination. N‑able partner stories show how MSPs use this model to add managed security without standing up a SOC. How to Choose a Threat Hunting Provider The right provider combines analyst-led methodology, multi-tenant fit, stack compatibility, measurable SLAs, and reporting that proves value over time. Analyst quality still separates real threat hunting from repackaged alert monitoring, but the evaluation has to go wider than that. Ask prospective providers to walk through a recent hunt, including the hypothesis, the data sources queried, and the outcome. If the answer centers entirely on automated detection without explaining how analysts form and test hypotheses, the service is monitoring under a different label. Beyond analyst expertise, five criteria matter most when evaluating providers: Hunting methodology: Providers should articulate a named, structured approach, such as hypothesis-driven or ATT&CK-mapped hunting, with documented playbooks. Behavioral analytics and anomaly detection must be core capabilities because sophisticated adversaries often leave few conventional indicators of compromise. Multi-tenancy architecture: For MSPs, logical data separation between client environments, role-based access control, per-client policy management, and white-label reporting are structural requirements. The play here is confirming whether the platform was purpose-built for multi-tenancy or adapted from a single-tenant product. Stack integration: Providers requiring full replacement of existing EDR or SIEM deployments can impose significant migration costs. The preferred model operates within your existing tooling instead of forcing a disruptive platform swap before hunting can begin. SLA specificity: Time-to-notify after a confirmed finding, time-to-investigate after escalation, and 24/7 consistency matter. Availability SLAs (“99.9% uptime”) are insufficient on their own because they do not show how quickly analysts validate and escalate real threats. Reporting depth: Reports must serve both technical teams and executive stakeholders, mapping findings to ATT&CK techniques while translating risk into business terms a CFO or board can act on. If reporting cannot show what was investigated, what was ruled out, and what changed after a hunt, it becomes difficult to prove value over time. Turn those criteria into a scorecard before the first demo. The questions and red-flag answers below give a starting framework: Criterion Question to ask Red flag answer Methodology Walk me through a recent hunt: hypothesis, data queried, outcome. Response centers on alert volume without hypothesis or outcome detail. Multi-tenancy Was the platform purpose-built for multi-tenancy, or adapted from a single-tenant product? Tenant separation is on the roadmap or requires manual configuration per client. Stack fit What existing tools must we replace before onboarding? Full EDR or SIEM migration required before any hunting begins. SLA What is your time-to-notify after a confirmed finding? Availability SLAs offered in place of finding-to-notify commitments. Reporting Show a recent report that includes negative findings and what was ruled out. Reports cover only positive detections, no audit-ready hunt documentation. Bottom line: if a provider cannot document negative findings and hunts that ruled out specific threats, it cannot demonstrate ongoing value during quiet periods or support compliance documentation of hunting frequency. The next section shows how those criteria map to the N‑able approach across protection, detection, and recovery. N‑able Threat Hunting Across the Attack Lifecycle Threat hunting works best when it connects to protection before an attack, response during an attack, and recovery after an attack. Standalone hunting raises detection quality, but durable attack resilience depends on closing the loop with prevention and recovery. The N‑able approach treats threat hunting as one layer within a complete before-during-after attack framework. Before an attack, N‑able N‑central hardens endpoints through automated patching, EDR, N‑able DNS Filtering , and vulnerability management. During an attack, Adlumin MDR/XDR detects and responds through 24/7 monitoring, automated detection, automated response, and threat hunting. title: Gross Margin for SaaS and Subscription Businesses Aug 2026
summary: Running a subscription business and not sure if your gross margin is actually good? The benchmark ranges that matter depend heavily on whether you're Sa...
body_text: Running a subscription business and not sure if your gross margin is actually good? The benchmark ranges that matter depend heavily on whether you're SaaS, e-commerce, or streaming, and most comparisons people reach for are too broad to be useful. Getting clear on the formula, what counts as COGS in your model, and where your number should sit gives you a far more accurate read on the health of your unit economics. TLDR: Gross margin (Revenue minus cost of goods sold (COGS), divided by revenue) sets the ceiling on every growth investment you can make. SaaS businesses typically run 70% to 85% gross margin; subscription e-commerce runs 30% to 50%; margins above 60% give you room to grow. Misclassifying operating expenses like sales or R&D as cost of goods sold (COGS) artificially suppresses your gross margin and distorts benchmarks. A 2% monthly involuntary churn rate on 50,000 subscribers means 1,000 lost subscribers per month, each carrying embedded customer acquisition cost (CAC) with no reduction in COGS. Slicker recovers failed-payment revenue through AI-powered smart retries and hyper-personalized dunning, with results proven via clinical-grade AABB testing on your own data before you commit. What Gross Margin Means in Business Gross margin tells you how much revenue remains after subtracting the direct costs of delivering your product or service. For subscription companies, those direct costs typically include hosting and infrastructure, customer success headcount tied to onboarding, payment processing fees, and third-party software embedded in the product. The number matters because it sets a ceiling on everything else. You cannot spend more on sales, marketing, or R&D than your gross margin allows and still reach profitability. A subscription business with 60% gross margin has far more room to grow than one running at 40%, even if both show identical top-line revenue. The Gross Margin Formula Gross margin is calculated by subtracting the cost of goods sold (COGS) from revenue, then dividing by revenue: Gross Margin % = (Revenue − COGS) / Revenue × 100 For a subscription company generating $1,000,000 in revenue with $300,000 in COGS, gross margin is 70%. That number tells you how much revenue remains to cover operating expenses, interest, and taxes before you reach net profit. What Counts as COGS for Subscription Businesses? COGS in a subscription context is narrower than most finance teams expect. It includes only the direct costs of delivering the service: Hosting and infrastructure costs tied directly to service delivery Customer support headcount allocated to onboarding and ongoing service Payment processing fees charged per transaction Third-party software or API costs embedded in the product Sales, marketing, R&D, and general administrative expenses sit below the gross margin line. Misclassifying those as COGS will artificially suppress your gross margin and distort benchmarking comparisons. Gross Margin vs. Gross Profit Gross margin and gross profit measure the same underlying relationship between revenue and cost of goods sold (COGS), but they express it differently. Gross profit is the raw dollar figure left after subtracting COGS from revenue. Gross margin converts that number into a percentage of revenue, making it comparable across companies of different sizes. For subscription businesses, the distinction matters because investors and operators almost always benchmark margin percentages, not absolute profit dollars. The Quick Comparison Metric Output Example ($1M revenue, $400K COGS) Gross Profit Dollar amount $600,000 Gross Margin Percentage 60% One tells you how many dollars your product generates above its direct costs. The other tells you how efficiently your business converts revenue into those dollars, which is what benchmarking, fundraising conversations, and board decks actually require. What COGS Includes for Subscription Companies For subscription businesses, cost of goods sold (COGS) looks different than in traditional product companies. Instead of raw materials or manufacturing costs, COGS covers the direct costs of delivering your service to customers. Common COGS line items include: Hosting and infrastructure costs (cloud compute, storage, CDN fees) that scale with your customer base Payment processing fees, including per-transaction charges from your payment processor Third-party software or API costs embedded in your product delivery Customer support costs directly tied to service delivery, such as onboarding and technical support headcount Expenses like sales, marketing, R&D, and general administration are operating expenses, not COGS. Keeping this separation clean is what makes gross margin a reliable signal of unit economics before overhead. Gross Margin vs. Operating Margin vs. Net Margin Gross margin stops at the cost of delivering your product. The two margins below it tell a fuller story about where revenue actually goes. The Three-Layer View These three margins sit at different points on the income statement: Gross margin measures revenue minus cost of goods sold (COGS), showing how much is left to cover all other expenses. Operating margin subtracts operating expenses like sales, marketing, and R&D from gross profit, revealing how much the business earns from its core activities before interest and taxes. Net margin takes everything out, including interest, taxes, and one-time items, producing the final bottom-line percentage. For subscription companies, gross margin tends to be the most stable of the three because it isolates unit economics from the spending choices a company makes on growth. Operating and net margins fluctuate far more with investment cycles, making gross margin the cleaner signal for assessing whether the underlying business model is sound. Why Gross Margin Matters More Than Revenue for Subscription Companies Revenue is a vanity metric if the unit economics underneath it are broken. A subscription company growing at 40% annually can still be destroying value if its gross margin sits at 30%, because there is simply not enough left over after fulfilling each subscription to cover sales, marketing, product, or any path to profitability. Gross margin tells you how much of each dollar of revenue survives the cost of delivering your product. For software-based subscription businesses, that surviving dollar funds everything else: customer acquisition, retention investment, and eventually, profit. Investors and operators track this number for good reason. SaaS businesses typically carry gross margins between 70% and 85%, while usage-heavy or service-heavy subscription models often run closer to 40% to 60%. A company at the low end of that range needs dramatically more revenue to reach the same operating performance as one at the high end. The implication for subscription companies is direct: protecting gross margin means protecting your ability to grow without proportionally growing your cost base. Factors That Can Compress Gross Margin For subscription companies, several structural cost pressures can quietly eat into gross margin over time. Infrastructure costs tend to scale with usage and not with revenue, so rapid subscriber growth can temporarily compress margins until engineering teams optimize resource consumption. Payment processing fees, including interchange and gateway costs, are typically treated as cost of revenue, reducing gross margin directly on every transaction. High support volume driven by onboarding friction or product complexity increases the cost of serving each customer, pulling margin down. Discounting and promotional pricing reduce recognized revenue without proportionally reducing delivery costs, which shrinks margin percentage even when subscriber counts grow. Tracking failed-payment analytics KPIs separately gives finance teams visibility into which cost categories are driving compression versus which reflect healthy growth investment. What Is a Good Gross Margin for Subscription Companies? Gross margin benchmarks vary meaningfully by business model, so subscription companies need sector-specific reference points, not broad industry averages. Benchmarks by Subscription Type The right target depends on what you deliver: Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) companies typically see gross margins between 70% and 85%, reflecting low incremental delivery costs once the product is built. Subscription e-commerce businesses (physical goods, boxes, consumables) generally run 30% to 50%, weighed down by product, packaging, and fulfillment costs. Streaming and digital media sit in the 50% to 70% range, with content licensing and delivery infrastructure as the primary cost drivers. What Signals a Healthy Margin A gross margin above 60% gives a subscription business enough headroom to invest in sales, marketing, and retention without compressing operating income. Margins below 40% leave little room for growth spending and tend to attract investor scrutiny at scale. The right benchmark is less about a single number and more about whether your margin supports the unit economics your customer acquisition cost (CAC) and lifetime value require. Your gross margin percentage is the starting point for that analysis, connecting directly to how much of each subscription dollar is available to cover the fixed costs that sit below the gross profit line. How Failed Payments Erode Gross Margin at Scale Every failed payment is a direct hit to gross margin. The revenue never arrives, but the cost to acquire and serve that subscriber already has. At scale, this gap compounds fast. Consider a subscription business with 50,000 active subscribers and a 2% monthly involuntary churn rate . That's 1,000 lost subscribers per month from failed payments alone, each carrying embedded customer acquisition cost (CAC), onboarding cost, and forgone lifetime value . None of those costs disappear when the payment fails. Recovering even a fraction of those failed payment losses moves the gross margin percentage meaningfully, without adding a single new customer. How Slicker Protects Gross Margin for Subscription Businesses Involuntary churn is one of the quietest destroyers of gross margin in subscription businesses. When a payment fails and a subscriber lapses, you lose the revenue you already earned without reducing your cost of goods sold (COGS). The margin on that lost subscriber simply disappears. Slicker recovers that revenue through AI-powered smart retries and hyper-personalized dunning, working silently on your existing billing infrastructure with zero engineering lift. Subscribers never know it happened. Your gross margin recovers alongside the revenue. The proof comes from your own data. Slicker runs clinical-grade AABB testing in payment recovery , splitting traffic 50/50 and measuring recovered dollars with statistical significance before you commit. If Slicker does not beat your control, you do not pay. Final Thoughts on Gross Margin and What It Means for Subscription Growth A strong gross margin percentage does not happen by accident. It comes from keeping COGS classification accurate, watching the cost categories that compress margin over time, and recovering every dollar of revenue your business already earned. The gap between a 60% and a 75% margin may sound small, but at scale it determines how much room you have to grow without burning cash. Get in touch if you want to see how much of your margin is slipping through failed payments. FAQ What is a good gross margin percentage for SaaS and subscription businesses? Gross margin benchmarks vary by business model: SaaS companies typically run 70% to 85%, streaming and digital media land in the 50% to 70% range, and subscription e-commerce sits closer to 30% to 50% due to fulfillment and product costs. A gross margin above 60% gives subscription businesses enough headroom to invest in sales, marketing, and retention without compressing operating income, while margins below 40% attract investor scrutiny at scale. What is the difference between gross margin, operating margin, and net margin for subscription companies? Gross margin measures revenue minus cost of goods sold (COGS), showing what remains before overhead. Operating margin subtracts sales, marketing, and R&D from gross profit, revealing what the core business earns before interest and taxes. Net margin takes out everything, including taxes and one-time items, producing the final bottom-line percentage. For subscription companies, gross margin is the most stable of the three because it isolates unit economics from growth-investment decisions. What counts as COGS in the gross margin formula for a SaaS or subscription business? COGS for subscription businesses covers only the direct costs of delivering the service: hosting and infrastructure, payment processing fees, third-party API costs embedded in the product, and customer support headcount tied to onboarding. Sales, marketing, R&D, and general administration are operating expenses that sit below the gross margin line. Misclassifying those as COGS artificially suppresses your gross margin and distorts any benchmarking comparison. How do failed payments affect gross margin, and can I recover that revenue without adding headcount? Every failed payment removes revenue you already earned while leaving your customer acquisition cost (CAC) and onboarding cost intact, directly compressing gross margin percentage at scale. Slicker recovers that revenue through AI-powered smart retries and hyper-personalized dunning that runs on your existing billing infrastructure, with zero engineering lift required. The recovery is silent: subscribers rarely know a payment failed, and the gross margin impact is proven against your own data through clinical-grade AABB testing before you pay anything. Gross margin vs net margin: which metric should subscription CFOs focus on when assessing business model health? Gross margin is the cleaner signal for assessing whether your underlying business model is sound, because it strips out variable growth spending that swings operating and net margin across investment cycles. Net margin tells you what survived after every cost, but a SaaS company burning on sales and marketing can show a near-zero net margin while carrying 80% gross margin, which signals a healthy unit economics foundation. Track gross margin as your primary business model health metric, and use operating and net margin to measure how efficiently you deploy the headroom it creates.

KRISPY KREME® Welcomes Fall with New Autumn Seasonal Collection on Aug. 11 08/07/2026 Download (opens in new window) Lineup features four craveable doughnuts and two seasonal beverages CHARLOTTE, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Move over, summer. Krispy Kreme® is welcoming the return of Pumpkin Spice – joined by the fan-favorite Biscoff® Cookie Butter Doughnut – as it unveils its Autumn Seasonal Collection , the brand's latest seasonal menu refresh, available beginning Tuesday, Aug. 11. Featuring the return of fan-favorite Pumpkin Spice alongside craveable new seasonal doughnuts and beverages, the lineup delivers the rich, comforting flavors fans wait all year to enjoy. And this is just the beginning, with even more seasonal experiences arriving later this month and throughout September. Lineup features four craveable doughnuts and two seasonal beverages Available for a limited time at participating shops nationwide, Krispy Kreme's Autumn Seasonal Collection features four doughnuts inspired by the season's most comforting flavors: NEW Maple Cheesecake Doughnut – An unglazed shell doughnut filled with cheesecake Kreme™, dipped in maple icing and topped with graham flavored crunch and maple drizzle. NEW Cafe Mocha Doughnut – An Original Glazed® doughnut dipped in chocolate icing and topped with a coffee flavored buttercreme swirl and a mocha bean. Biscoff® Cookie Butter Doughnut – An unglazed shell doughnut filled with Biscoff Cookie Butter Kreme™, dipped in Biscoff cookie butter icing and topped with Biscoff cookie pieces, then drizzled with white icing. Pumpkin Spice Cake Doughnut – An Original Glazed® Old Fashioned cake doughnut featuring pumpkin spice flavor. Krispy Kreme is also serving up two seasonal lattes that celebrate the flavors of fall: Pumpkin Spice Latte – A latte flavored with pumpkin pie sauce, topped with whipped cream and pumpkin spice seasoning. NEW Apple Crisp Latte – A latte flavored with apple crisp syrup, topped with whipped cream, caramel drizzle and graham flavored topping. "Nobody welcomes fall quite like Krispy Kreme, and we're excited to bring back Pumpkin Spice while introducing even more seasonal flavors for our fans to fall in love with," said Alison Holder, Chief Product and Brand Officer at Krispy Kreme . "Whether you're team Pumpkin Spice, maple, mocha or Biscoff® Cookie Butter, our Autumn Seasonal Collection has something for every fall craving. And we're just getting started." Krispy Kreme’s Autumn Seasonal Collection will be available in-shop and for pickup or delivery via Krispy Kreme's app and website, individually and by the dozen, while supplies last. Visit www.krispykreme.com/locate/location-search to find a shop near you. Share how you're cozying up to fall with Krispy Kreme’s new Autumn Seasonal Collection by using #KrispyKreme and tagging @krispykreme on social media. About Krispy Kreme Headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., Krispy Kreme is one of the most beloved and well-known sweet treat brands in the world. Our iconic Original Glazed® doughnut is universally recognized for its hot-off-the-line, melt-in-your-mouth experience. Krispy Kreme operates in more than 40 countries through its unique network of fresh doughnut shops, partnerships with leading retailers, and a rapidly growing digital business. Our purpose of touching and enhancing lives through the joy that is Krispy Kreme guides how we operate every day and is reflected in the love we have for our people, our communities, and the planet. title: Warner Music Group Internship 2027–2028: Programs, Deadlines & How to Apply
summary: Warner Music Group internship guide for 2027-2028: WMG's paid Emerging Talent Associate (ETA) Program, deadlines, $17-18.42/hr pay, and how to get in.
body_text: Warner Music Group Internship 2027–2028: Programs, Deadlines & How to Apply Last updated: August 2026 Warner Music Group's Emerging Talent Associate Program receives thousands of applications each semester for a limited number of placements, while the company itself generated $6.7 billion in fiscal-2025 revenue and holds an estimated 15% share of the global recorded-music market. Here is everything you need to know to land one of those seats for summer 2027. Quick Facts Fact Detail Where to apply wmg.com/emerging-talent ; apply via Workday (wmg.wd1.myworkdayjobs.com/WMGUS). Follow @wmgearlycareers on Instagram for window openings Application window (2027–28) Not posted yet. Summer 2027 applications expected to open ~March 2027 with a deadline ~mid-April 2027 (expected), projected from Summer 2026 (deadline April 17, 2026). Other windows: Spring (Nov–Jan), Fall (Jul–Aug) Rolling? Yes. WMG reviews ETA applications on a rolling basis and urges applying as early as possible; placements can fill before the posted deadline Eligibility 18+ by program start, located in the U.S. for the full program, own housing and transportation. Open to degree- and non-degree-seeking applicants; credit available. Business & Legal Affairs requires pursuing a J.D.; Creative roles require a portfolio Duration Semester-length; ~10 weeks for summer (Summer 2026 offered May 18–Jul 24, May 26–Jul 31, or Jun 1–Aug 7). Part-time: 20-25 hrs/week, up to 29 in summer Compensation $17.00–$18.42/hour (employer-provided on ETA postings). Housing not provided. Academic credit available. Ignore inflated Glassdoor aggregate estimates; the JD figures are authoritative Return offers No official conversion rate published (not found). Community reports show ETAs returning across semesters ("returning intern"), indicating a recognized pipeline into coordinator and entry-level roles Locations New York, Los Angeles, Nashville, and Miami. Hybrid (mostly onsite). You must be located in the U.S. for the entire program # Programs One umbrella program, the Emerging Talent Associate (ETA) Program, running Spring, Summer, and Fall cohorts across 20+ department placements (A&R, Marketing, Sync, Finance, Data Analytics, and more) Warner Music Group runs one paid internship, the Emerging Talent Associate (ETA) Program, with Spring, Summer, and Fall cohorts across 20+ department placements. It pays $17.00-$18.42/hour, is part-time (20-25 hrs/week) and hybrid across NY, LA, Nashville, and Miami, uses a rolling application plus a video-interview screen, and does not provide housing. Summer 2027 applications are expected to open around March 2027. Externships are short, remote projects where you finish real work for a real company. The TikTok Social Media Content & Brand Strategy Externship and the Beats by Dre Consumer Behavior Externship build the marketing, audience-insight, and brand-storytelling evidence that WMG's music-obsessed ETA application rewards. Explore all Externships . What Is a Warner Music Group Internship? Warner Music Group is one of the three major recorded-music companies in the world, home to Atlantic Records, Warner Records, Elektra, 300 Entertainment, and publishing giant Warner Chappell Music. It generated $6.7 billion in fiscal-2025 revenue, employs about 5,500 people across 70+ countries, and holds roughly a 15% share of the global recorded-music market. Its early-career front door is the Emerging Talent Associate (ETA) Program: a paid, part-time, semester-long internship that runs three cohorts a year (Spring, Summer, and Fall) and places associates across A&R, marketing, digital, sync, finance, data analytics, promotion, publicity, and more. Unlike a single fixed internship, the ETA Program is an umbrella that spans dozens of department placements across Warner's labels and business units, so "a WMG internship" really means picking the track and label that fit your goals, then applying into that specific placement. It is hybrid, based in New York, Los Angeles, Nashville, or Miami, and famously competitive: WMG says it receives thousands of applications each semester for a limited number of seats. When Do Warner Music Group Internship Applications Open for 2027–2028? Warner Music Group has not posted Summer 2027 ETA roles yet, but the cycle is predictable. WMG runs three application windows a year, Spring (November-January), Summer (March-April), and Fall (July-August), and recruits on a rolling basis inside each. For Summer 2026, applications opened in March 2026 and closed April 17, 2026, with the program running roughly May through August. Projecting that forward, Summer 2027 applications are expected to open around March 2027 with a deadline near mid-April 2027 (expected). Because review is rolling and placements can fill before the deadline, the build window is now: develop music-business fluency, build a portfolio, and follow @wmgearlycareers so you catch the exact open date. Now · Summer 2026 YOU ARE HERE The Summer 2026 window has closed and that cohort is wrapping up. This is the build window for summer 2027: get fluent in WMG's labels, build a marketing or audience-insight portfolio, and follow @wmgearlycareers so you catch the next open date. The TikTok Social Media Content & Brand Strategy Externship and the Beats by Dre Consumer Behavior Externship are remote, real-company projects that give you finished marketing and audience-insight work to point at in a WMG application. Fall 2026 to Winter 2027 Preparation window. Build a resume tailored to a specific track and label, draft authentic written and video short-answers, and assemble a portfolio if you are targeting a Creative placement. The Fall 2026 cohort (window ~Jul-Aug 2026) may still have visible postings if you want a nearer-term entry. ~March 2027 (expected) EXPECTED ROLLING — APPLY WEEK 1 Summer 2027 applications expected to open (Summer window is March-April). Because recruitment is rolling and placements can fill before the deadline, submit in the first days of the window, not the last. April to May 2027 (expected) EXPECTED Application deadline expected ~mid-April 2027 (Summer 2026 was April 17). Then a HireVue-style recorded video interview, a live Zoom or in-person round (1:1 and/or panel) with the hiring manager, and rolling offers, mirroring the documented Summer 2025 cycle. June 2027 (expected) Summer 2027 program starts, running roughly 10 weeks through August with staggered start/end options. Hybrid and mostly onsite in New York, Los Angeles, Nashville, or Miami; you arrange your own housing. Why You Must Apply the Week Applications Open WMG states plainly that ETA recruitment is "conducted on a rolling basis" and that you should "apply as soon as possible for your best shot at landing a role." That is not boilerplate. Because thousands of applications arrive each semester for a limited number of placements, and because hiring managers can extend offers before the posted deadline, a strong application submitted in week one is read while seats are still open; the same application submitted in week five may land after a placement is already filled. The documented Summer 2025 cycle shows how fast it moves once you are in: a HireVue-style video-interview invite went out April 30, a live Zoom interview followed May 19, and an offer landed May 23, roughly four days later. So the play for summer 2027 is simple: have your resume, written and video short-answers, and (for Creative roles) portfolio ready before applications open around March 2027, then submit in the first days of the window. Which Warner Music Group Internship Programs Should You Target? WMG does not brand separate "programs." Instead, the single Emerging Talent Associate Program spans dozens of placements that cluster into a handful of tracks. The Summer 2026 Atlantic Music Group posting alone listed 20+ distinct placements across 10K Projects, 300 Entertainment, and Atlantic Records, with additional postings per label and division. Here are the tracks to target, all drawn from real Summer 2026 ETA placement lists: Track Focus Example placements Locations A&R Artist scouting, A&R research, roster support, demo and data review Atlantic Records A&R, 300 Entertainment A&R, 10K Projects A&R, Warner Records A&R NY, LA (hybrid) Marketing / Digital / Product Management Release marketing, digital and influencer strategy, streaming and playlist strategy, product management Atlantic Digital Marketing, Influencer Marketing, Innovative Marketing, 300 Ent Marketing NY, LA (hybrid) Promotion, Publicity & Press/Media Strategy Radio and DSP promotion, publicity, press and media strategy Atlantic Promotion, Press & Media Strategy NY (hybrid) Sync, Creative & Content Protection Music licensing for film/TV/ads, clearance, content protection, video and graphic design (portfolio required for Creative) Global Sync, Creative Sync, Clearance, Atlantic Creative LA (hybrid) Finance & Data Analytics FP&A support, royalty and financial operations, streaming and audience data analytics Finance and Data Analytics placements across divisions NY, LA, Nashville (hybrid) Business & Legal Affairs (J.D.-only) Contracts, rights, clearances, business affairs Business & Legal Affairs placements NY (hybrid) See live placements on the WMG Emerging Talent page and apply through Workday. Note that WMG requires a fresh application each semester and each hiring manager runs their own interview process, so target the specific label and track that fits your goals rather than applying generically. What Are the Eligibility Requirements? The ETA Program's eligibility is refreshingly open compared with most brand-name internships, but a few requirements are firm. From the official WMG Emerging Talent page and Summer 2026 ETA job descriptions: • Age: At least 18 years old by the start of the program. • Location: You must be located within the United States for the entire duration of the program. • Housing and transportation: You must have your own access to housing and transportation within the designated city. WMG does not provide housing or relocation. • Commitment: Part-time, 20-25 hours per week (up to 29 hours per week during the Summer semester). This is not a 40-hour internship, and many ETAs combine it with school. • Student status: Open to both degree-seeking and non-degree-seeking individuals; academic credit is available for those who need it. • Disposition: A self-starter attitude, genuine curiosity for the business, and a real passion for and knowledge of the music industry. • Department exceptions: Business & Legal Affairs placements require actively pursuing a law degree (J.D.); Creative placements (graphic design, video, motion graphics, content creation) require a portfolio. Do You Have to Be a Current College Student? No, and that is one of the program's most distinctive features. The ETA Program is open to both degree-seeking and non-degree-seeking applicants aged 18 and over, so you do not have to be currently enrolled to apply, though academic credit is available for students who want it. Two caveats matter. First, Business & Legal Affairs is J.D.-gated: those placements are reserved for people actively pursuing a law degree. Second, Creative placements require a submitted portfolio. Beyond that, WMG weighs showed passion for and knowledge of its specific labels and business units far more than pedigree, and it requires a fresh application each semester, so prior applicants are encouraged to re-apply. Generic, label-agnostic applications consistently underperform. What Skills Does Warner Music Group Look For, and How Do You Build Them? WMG's ETA job descriptions are intentionally general, because one posting often covers many departments, so they lead with transferable strengths rather than narrow technical stacks. Across the recurring "It would be music to our ears" requirements block that appears on ETA postings, the same qualities repeat: excellent written and verbal communication, effective problem-solving, organizational skills to juggle multiple priorities, leadership experience, and, above all, a strong passion for and knowledge of the music industry and WMG's specific labels. Role-specific technical skills (SQL and data-viz for Data Analytics, Adobe Creative Suite for Creative, legal research for Business & Legal Affairs) are implied by the placement rather than spelled out in the umbrella JD. What the application actually tests is communication and genuine music-business fluency, expressed through written and video short-answers that WMG's Talent Acquisition team reviews personally. What Warner Music Group looks for in interns Skills across 6 Warner Music Group intern & analyst job descriptions · Summer & Fall 2026 WMG ETA postings (Atlantic Music Group, Global Sync, Warner divisions), cross-checked vs. aggregate media-intern JDs; projecting Summer 2027 Verbal & written communication 6 of 6 Passion for & knowledge of the music industry 6 of 6 Knowledge of WMG's labels & business units 6 of 6 Organizational skills / juggling priorities 6 of 6 Effective problem-solving 5 of 6 Self-starter attitude & curiosity 5 of 6 Leadership experience (on/off campus) 5 of 6 MS Office + social/digital content fluency 4 of 6 Goals aligned with WMG's core values 4 of 6 Method: analysis of the recurring WMG ETA requirements block across Summer and Fall 2026 postings (Atlantic Music Group, Global Sync, and Warner divisions), cross-checked against an aggregate media/entertainment-intern JD snapshot. The umbrella JD is deliberately general, so most core requirements appear on nearly every posting; the Microsoft Office and social-content line is drawn from the aggregate media-intern data and is strongest for Marketing, Digital, and Creative placements. How Is Demand for Media & Entertainment Interns Moving Right Now? Media & entertainment intern hiring right now: August 2026 Across US media/entertainment intern postings tracked this month · aggregate market data, all employers = About 45 US entertainment-industry summer-internship postings were open on Indeed's headline query in August 2026, a seasonal trough; media and entertainment intern hiring peaks October-January for the following summer cycle ★ Media intern pay clusters low: entertainment-industry interns average about $17.04/hr, social-media interns about $16.65/hr, and digital-media interns about $14.83/hr on ZipRecruiter aggregates, right in line with WMG's $17-$18.42/hr ETA rate ▲ Scripted-TV peers pay more: AMC Networks' Summer 2026 interns earned $20/hr for most tracks ($25/hr for J.D. legal), and Microsoft Office plus social/content fluency (TikTok, Instagram, X) dominates the skills these media JDs screen for August is a seasonal trough for media internships; the real surge comes October-January for summer 2027. The signal today is level pay in the mid-teens per hour, so WMG's $17-$18.42 ETA rate is competitive for the field, if a notch below scripted-TV peers like AMC Networks. Method: aggregate analysis of US entertainment/media, social-media, and digital-media intern postings via ZipRecruiter, Indeed, and Glassdoor plus real media-company intern JDs (AMC Networks Summer 2026), August 2026 baseline. The sample indexes a fraction of all US postings, so figures show direction and relative level, not total market share. Build These Skills Before You Apply And the skills in that chart map directly to remote Externships where you finish a real music, marketing, or audience-insight project before applications even open. Skill (from real JDs) JD evidence Externship that builds it Marketing, digital & social-media strategy ETA JDs: "digital marketing," "influencer marketing," "innovative marketing," plus MS Office and TikTok/Instagram/X fluency across Marketing and Digital placements TikTok Social Media Content & Brand Strategy Audience & consumer insight (A&R research, market analysis) ETA JDs: A&R research and roster support, "passion for and knowledge of the music industry," streaming and audience data review Beats by Dre Consumer Behavior Product & content innovation, fan engagement ETA JDs: Content Creation, Innovative Marketing, video content and product-management placements BeReal Product Innovation How close is the overlap? The TikTok project hands you a finished brand campaign that mirrors the digital-marketing placements WMG fills most, and the Beats consumer-insight work builds the audience-to-decision story an A&R or marketing interviewer wants to hear. What Is the Warner Music Group Application and Interview Process Like? The ETA process is not a coding gauntlet; it is a music-business and communication filter. From the WMG Emerging Talent page's official candidate process: 1. Watch for the window. Follow @wmgearlycareers on Instagram and WMG on LinkedIn. Applications go live each semester, with the Summer window opening around March. 2. Apply via Workday. Submit through the WMG "Apply Now" link (wmg.wd1.myworkdayjobs.com/WMGUS) as early as possible, because review is rolling. 3. Submit your resume. A resume is required for every placement. 4. Answer the short-answer questions, written and video. WMG's Talent Acquisition team personally reviews every response, so make them authentic and specific to the label and role. 5. Submit a portfolio if you are applying to a Creative placement. 6. If selected, the hiring manager reaches out directly with their own interview process, which varies by team. 7. Complete at least one interview , video-recorded (HireVue-style) and/or a live Zoom or in-person round, as a 1:1 with the hiring manager and/or a panel. 8. Follow up politely if you have not heard back by the stated date. A single follow-up after about a week is fine per WMG's guidance. Two things to note. First, there is no standardized aptitude or LeetCode-style test; the "assessment" is the application itself plus a recorded video-interview step. Second, the process can move quickly once a hiring manager is engaged: in the documented Summer 2025 cycle, a candidate went from an April 30 video-interview invite to a May 23 offer. Prep by researching your interviewer on LinkedIn, knowing WMG's labels and latest Impact Report, and being ready to explain why this role, why WMG, and how it fits your goals. Three moves, all executable before applications open. First, get specific about WMG's labels and business units: the JDs and the interview both reward candidates who can talk credibly about Atlantic, Warner Records, 300 Entertainment, or Warner Chappell and why a particular one fits, so pick a track and a label rather than applying as a generic "music fan." Second, treat the written and video short-answers as the real assessment, because they are; WMG's Talent Acquisition team reviews every response personally, so authentic, specific answers about why this role and why WMG beat polished-but-generic ones. Third, build finished proof of the skill your target track needs: a real marketing campaign, an audience-insight deck, or (for Creative) a portfolio you can submit. A remote Externship is a fast way to manufacture that evidence, so you walk in with a shipped project instead of just enthusiasm. What Other Companies Should You Consider? WMG is one of three major music companies, and its ETA Program competes with the early-career pipelines at the other majors and across the wider live-music and streaming world. If you are building a music and media internship list, these are the obvious neighbors: Universal Music Group The largest of the three major labels (Interscope, Republic, Def Jam), with its own early-career and internship pipeline Careers site Sony Music Entertainment The third major, home to Columbia and RCA, running structured internships across labels and corporate functions Careers site Live Nation Entertainment The dominant live-music and ticketing company (Ticketmaster), with large internship cohorts across touring, venues, and marketing Careers site Spotify The leading music-streaming platform and a top destination for music-data, marketing, and product interns Guide → iHeartMedia The largest US audio company (radio and podcasts), with internships across marketing, promotion, and digital Guide → Want the fastest way to build the exact skills these companies screen for? Browse all Externships to finish a real music, marketing, or audience-insight project before the next application window opens. FAQ Can I still apply for a summer 2026 Warner Music Group internship? The Summer 2026 window has closed: applications were due April 17, 2026, and the program itself ran from mid-May through August 2026. Your realistic next chances are the Fall 2026 cohort (WMG's Fall window runs roughly July-August, so late postings may still be visible) and, for a full summer, the Summer 2027 cohort, which is expected to open around March 2027. Follow @wmgearlycareers so you catch the exact open date, and because review is rolling, apply in the first days of whichever window you target. Does Warner Music Group offer internships? Yes, through the paid Emerging Talent Associate (ETA) Program, offered every Spring, Summer, and Fall across departments including A&R, Marketing, Finance, Data Analytics, Sync, Promotion, and more. It is a part-time, semester-long, hybrid program based in New York, Los Angeles, Nashville, and Miami. When do Summer 2027 applications open? They are not posted yet. Based on Summer 2026 (deadline April 17, 2026) and WMG's stated Summer window of March-April, Summer 2027 applications are expected to open around March 2027 with a deadline near mid-April 2027 (expected). Follow @wmgearlycareers for the exact date, and apply early because recruitment is rolling. How much do WMG interns get paid? $17.00-$18.42 per hour on actual ETA postings (employer-provided figures). Hours are 20-25 per week, up to 29 during the summer. Housing is not provided, and academic credit is available. Ignore the inflated Glassdoor aggregate "intern" estimates; the employer-provided JD figures are authoritative. Where are WMG internships located? New York, Los Angeles, Nashville, and Miami, run as a hybrid program that is mostly onsite. You must be located in the United States for the entire program and arrange your own housing and transportation in the designated city. Do I have to be a current college student? No. The ETA Program is open to both degree-seeking and non-degree-seeking individuals aged 18 and over, and academic credit is available for students who want it. The exception is Business & Legal Affairs, which requires actively pursuing a J.D. Creative placements also require a portfolio. What does the application involve? A resume plus written and video short-answer responses submitted through Workday, and a portfolio for Creative placements. WMG's Talent Acquisition team personally reviews every response, so specificity about the label and role matters more than polish. What is the interview process like? It varies by hiring manager but includes at least one interview, often a recorded HireVue-style video screen followed by a live Zoom or in-person round (a 1:1 with the hiring manager and/or a panel). Some interviews run as short as 15 minutes, and offers can arrive within days of the live round. WMG's ETA Program takes thousands of applications a semester for a handful of seats, so the students who get in show up already fluent in the music business. Spend the runway building proof: a remote Externship like TikTok's Social Media Content & Brand Strategy project turns "I love music" into a finished brand campaign you can point a hiring manager to. Over 7 years at Extern, he has had one-on-one sessions with thousands of students exploring careers in consulting, finance, tech, marketing, and data, giving him a firsthand view of how the job market has shifted for early-career professionals and what it actually takes to break in.
